            "This thought experiment is useful because it exposes what the license is actually trying to protect.\n\nSuppose in 1650 this person has, in recognizable conceptual form, something approaching the electrical field/current/electromagnetic synthesis that historically took centuries to assemble. He also has modern publication, licensing, patent, and corporate institutions available. And his preference is roughly: “this is structure of nature; nobody should own electricity.”\n\nThen there are several very different mistakes he could make.\n\nThe first would be to keep it XXXXXXX. That preserves control but catastrophically reduces diffusion and delays whatever social benefit the work could produce.\n\nThe second would be to publish everything under something MIT-like. That maximizes diffusion, but it also gives every future industrial actor permission to take his copyrightable materials, documentation, software, diagrams, and implementations into closed commercial systems with essentially no obligation beyond whatever attribution the license requires. And publication would likely destroy many of his own opportunities to patent implementations while simultaneously creating prior art against later patents by others.\n\nThe third would be to put everything under “noncommercial only.” That protects against enclosure more strongly, but it creates a bizarre result. The telegraph company, electrical utility, medical-device manufacturer, university spinout, industrial motor company, and semiconductor company all have to negotiate merely because their work is commercial. The people most capable of turning the discovery into civilization-scale infrastructure encounter friction precisely when you want adoption.\n\nSo our hypothetical Ampère-Maxwell-in-1650 probably teaches us that the desirable distinction isn't:\n\n> commercial / noncommercial.\n\nIt is:\n\n> **commons-preserving use / commons-extracting use.**\n\nThat's a much better axis.\n\nImagine what he might actually want.\n\nA village builds a generator from his diagrams and charges enough to maintain it: great.\n\nAn engineer starts a company producing safer motors: great.\n\nA university patents some highly specific engineering improvement and licenses it while publishing the science: probably fine.\n\nA huge industrial concern builds its entire electrical empire on the framework, patents every implementation it can surround it with, prevents competitors from entering, stops publishing improvements, erases the intellectual lineage, and accumulates enormous rents from controlling access to something whose enabling intellectual structure was freely given to humanity:\n\nThat's the case that violates his intention.\n\nAnd notice that **citation alone doesn't solve that case**.\n\nSuppose General Electric puts this on page 943 of an annual report:\n\n> “The foundational electromagnetic framework was originally developed by A. Weirdguy (1650).”\n\nThey have now attributed him perfectly while still enclosing the entire technological ecosystem.\n\nLikewise, compensation alone doesn't solve it. They could send him $10 million and then monopolize electrification. He might regard that as even worse.\n\nSo the maximum-impact thought experiment suggests that your policy has at least three independent variables:\n\n**Attribution.** Don't erase provenance.\n\n**Access/contribution.** Don't take an open intellectual commons and turn the consequential downstream knowledge completely opaque.\n\n**Compensation.** Once enormous private value is being extracted from a contribution freely supplied to the commons, some return to the contributor or commons becomes reasonable.\n\nAnd those don't have to kick in at the same threshold.\n\nThat suggests something like a graduated regime rather than one switch.\n\nAt the bottom:\n\n**Ordinary use — essentially unrestricted.**\n\nRead it. Teach it. Calculate from it. Write papers about it. Criticize it. Build prototypes. Start a small company. Make a product. Cite reasonably where there is an identifiable SAT contribution.\n\nNo payment. No permission request.\n\nAt the middle:\n\n**Material commercial dependence — provenance obligation becomes stronger.**\n\nIf a product, research program, patent, or commercial methodology materially depends upon identifiable SAT/RMS/H(s)H structures, don't merely bury a generic archive URL somewhere. Identify the relevant antecedent in a technically useful way.\n\nStill potentially no payment.\n\nAt the top:\n\n**Large-scale private extraction — reciprocal obligation appears.**\n\nNow the user gets choices rather than a prohibition.\n\nThey could:\n\n- keep important resulting technical knowledge openly available;\n- contribute substantial improvements back to the public research commons;\n- provide some negotiated compensation;\n- provide broad public access to the resulting technology;\n- or negotiate some mixture of those.\n\nThis is where your teleport-booth example starts making sense.\n\nImagine the 1650 discoverer's terms had ultimately produced an electric utility worth $500 billion. Asking the utility to acknowledge him would be absurdly inadequate. Asking it to pay him 30% of electricity revenue would be socially destructive. Saying “nobody may sell electricity” would also be socially destructive.\n\nBut saying something like:\n\n> You were permitted to build freely from this publicly disclosed foundation. Once that foundation becomes materially responsible for a very large closed commercial position, your obligation is either to preserve meaningful public access to the resulting knowledge or to negotiate a reasonable return.\n\nThat's not crazy at all.\n\nAnd I think it identifies what you've been calling **consolidation** much better.\n\nConsolidation isn't just a citation.\n\nIt's maintaining the relationship between:\n\n**source → development → consequential derivative.**\n\nThe source doesn't disappear when the derivative becomes lucrative.\n\nThere is another important lesson from the 1650 scenario: **patents become much more important than copyright at maximum impact.**\n\nIf this man merely CC-licenses *Principia Electrica*, copyright governs his particular text, illustrations, arrangement, etc. It does not give him ownership of electromagnetic induction.\n\nOnce another person understands the principle and designs a motor independently, copyright has very little to say about it.\n\nIf he genuinely wants to prevent somebody else from enclosing the newly discovered technological landscape, the powerful move isn't primarily copyright licensing. It is some combination of:\n\n**early public disclosure**, which can destroy later attempts to patent already-disclosed things;\n\nand perhaps\n\n**strategic patents on specific implementations**, held not as private monopolies but by some trust or foundation operating under a public-benefit licensing policy.\n\nThat creates a fascinating 1650 strategy.\n\nOur imaginary inventor could establish something like an **Electromagnetic Commons Trust**.\n\nHe transfers qualifying patents to it.\n\nThe trust promises:\n\n> Anyone may use these inventions royalty-free for research, education, personal use, public infrastructure, open implementation, and qualifying small enterprise.\n\nLarge closed commercial users receive licenses too, but under reciprocal conditions.\n\nAnd the trust itself is prohibited from selling exclusive control over the fundamental portfolio.\n\nThat's much closer to “skip cXXXtalism” than merely stamping **NONCOMMERCIAL** on a PDF.\n\nIt doesn't prohibit markets. It tries to stop the discovery from becoming an artificial chokepoint.\n\nNow bring that back to SAT.\n\nThe maximum-impact version of SAT isn't “a paper becomes influential.”\n\nIt's something like:\n\nSAT's representational grammar turns out to expose an unusually productive way of seeing several previously disconnected domains; somebody subsequently gets quantum computation, energy technology, materials engineering, whatever, to work much better because the geometry makes certain transformations obvious.\n\nIn that situation I think the thing you'd most regret is **not** failing to collect a $50 citation fee in 2026.\n\nYou'd regret creating terms that meant:\n\n> I intentionally gave everybody permission to privatize every consequential derivative while retaining no meaningful mechanism for either acknowledgment, reciprocity, or participation.\n\nBut the opposite mistake would be:\n\n> I made the framework sufficiently legally awkward that nobody serious touched it.\n\nSo the 1650 experiment pushes me away from a simple permanent **CC BY-NC** solution.\n\nI think the eventual architecture probably wants to be:\n\n**Very open research license + explicit provenance norm + standing generous commercial safe harbor + reciprocal/open-or-negotiate condition only at substantial scale.**\n\nAnd perhaps later, completely separately:\n\n**a patent/publication policy for genuinely operationalizable inventions.**\n\nThat last piece doesn't have to exist today.\n\nBut I think we've learned something important about the unresolved threshold question.\n\nThe trigger shouldn't primarily be **“you made money.”**\n\nThe trigger should be closer to:\n\n> **A substantial private economic position has become materially dependent upon an identifiable contribution from the archive while the resulting development is being kept substantially closed.**\n\nThen scale tells us when that becomes worth enforcing.\n\nThat is a considerably better definition of the thing you've actually been objecting to. memcite"

            "Yes. That clarifies the target much more sharply.\n\nYou are not really trying to reserve a personal royalty stream. You are trying to use whatever leverage the archive happens to possess to prevent a one-way conversion:\n\n> **commons → insight → private asymmetry → permanent tollbooth**\n\nWhat you want instead is:\n\n> **commons → insight → productive activity → enough return flow to keep the commons buoyant**\n\nSo Kircher can give electricity away. He doesn't demand a penny every time somebody closes a circuit. But if electricity becomes the foundation of an enormous private industrial apparatus, the grant under which that apparatus uses his protected contribution says, in effect:\n\n> You don't owe *me* electricity rent.  \n> You owe the commons some circulation.\n\nThat means our earlier “open or compensate Nathan” construction is actually slightly wrong. Compensation to you can remain an option, but it shouldn't be the conceptual center.\n\nI think the license needs something like a **Commons Reciprocity Condition**.\n\nFor individuals, scholarship, education, nonprofits, hobbyists, independent researchers, ordinary publication, experimentation, small businesses, prototypes, etc.: essentially no friction beyond reasonable provenance.\n\nThen at the still-undecided threshold where a commercial use becomes a **substantial private economic dependency** on the licensed corpus, the user gets several ways to satisfy reciprocity. Something along these lines:\n\n> A Qualifying Commercial User may continue commercial use by making a meaningful Commons Contribution through one or more of the following:\n>\n> - making consequential resulting knowledge, research, specifications, or implementations openly available;\n> - providing the resulting SAT-derived capability broadly to the public on free or strongly public-benefit terms;\n> - contributing an agreed portion of resulting value to an independent public-benefit/commons mechanism;\n> - granting appropriate royalty-free rights for public, humanitarian, educational, basic-needs, or commons uses;\n> - or entering another agreement reasonably accomplishing the same purpose.\n\nThat's much closer to **“want computers, give me Kropotkin.”**\n\nAnd importantly, the license needn't say *Kropotkin*. The politics can be expressed operationally rather than ideologically. Someone doesn't have to agree with your economic philosophy. They just have to satisfy the condition attached to the additional commercial permission you're offering.\n\nI would make the purpose statement unusually explicit, though:\n\n> **The purpose of the Commons Reciprocity Condition is not to suppress commerce, require uncompensated labor, or prohibit private profit. Its purpose is to prevent substantial private enclosure of value derived from research deliberately contributed to the public commons without a meaningful return flow to that commons.**\n\nThat is almost exactly your buoyancy-engine model.\n\nIt also suggests that **“commercial/noncommercial” is not really the fundamental distinction**. There are probably three regimes:\n\n**Open use.** Basically everybody starts here. No negotiation.\n\n**Commercial safe harbor.** Companies can make money, sell things, patent genuinely new engineering, employ people, etc., provided the exploitation remains below whatever substantiality threshold we eventually choose. Citation/provenance remains expected.\n\n**Commons-reciprocal commercial use.** Once the use becomes sufficiently economically important and sufficiently dependent upon the archive, continued licensed exploitation requires some return flow. The licensee gets flexibility about its form.\n\nThat last flexibility matters enormously. Google shouldn't be required to open-source a teleporter if doing so would, say, immediately enable people to teleport nuclear weapons. There needs to be an alternative route. Maybe they fund universal deployment. Maybe they license the technology royalty-free for public infrastructure. Maybe they contribute some tiny fraction of enormous revenues to a commons trust. Maybe they make the underlying research open while keeping safety-critical engineering controlled.\n\nThe **outcome** is mandatory; the exact form needn't be.\n\nAnd I think we have just found a better word than “consolidation” for the policy itself:\n\n**reciprocity.**\n\n“Consolidation” was useful for getting at the thought, but it can sound like bibliography or accounting. What you're talking about is a **reciprocal commons relationship**.\n\nThere is a hard limit that remains: an archive copyright license cannot make the universe itself subject to this covenant. Someone independently discovering the same physical principle generally doesn't become bound merely because SAT disclosed it first. Likewise, copyright doesn't automatically control a newly invented machine implementing an unprotectable idea. So the maximum-impact version of the strategy eventually has three possible pieces:\n\n> **publication/provenance** prevents historical disappearance and helps prevent others from patenting what was already publicly disclosed;\n>\n> **copyright/database/software licensing** governs actual use of protected archive materials and tools;\n>\n> **specific patent rights, where ever deliberately retained**, could carry the strongest commons-reciprocity conditions on actual technological implementations.\n\nYou don't have to build the third apparatus now. But if Kircher suddenly realizes tomorrow that one particular SAT derivation actually describes a working battery rather than merely the principles of electricity, that's the moment to decide before publishing the construction details.\n\nThere is another consequence that I think fits your ethics especially well: **the commercial payment destination need not ultimately be you.**\n\nA future clause could say that once some very-high threshold is crossed, monetary reciprocity can be satisfied through payment to:\n\n**[NATHAN / DESIGNATED COMMONS TRUST / PUBLIC-BENEFIT FUND / OTHER — TBD]**\n\nThat preserves your ability to benefit—you shouldn't have to become the one person excluded from the abundance your own work helped produce—without turning the system into “Nathan owns a tax on electricity.”\n\nAt maximum success, you could even envision the rights eventually sitting in an independent **SB2325 Commons Trust**, with a charter saying its purpose is to convert whatever economic leverage the corpus produces into reduced obligatory scarcity: food, housing, health, infrastructure, basic security, knowledge access, etc.\n\nThen the extreme hypothetical becomes quite elegant:\n\n**Kircher doesn't own electricity.**\n\n**General Electric doesn't get to own Kircher's gift either.**\n\n**Electricity helps pay for the conditions under which nobody has to sell their Tuesday afternoon merely to remain alive.**\n\nThat, I think, is the principle our final licensing architecture should be designed around."

You did **not** thereby volunteer to be personally excluded from the value if somebody systematically mines that work into a major commercial technology stack.\n\nSo the high-impact principle should be:\n\n> **Open intellectual use by default; meaningful personal participation when identifiable SAT-derived value becomes substantially commercial; and, at very large scale, some additional return to the commons.**\n\nThose are three different things.\n\nA researcher finding one useful SAT idea and building a product should not suddenly owe you half their company. A company deliberately combing the archive, following its conceptual grammar, formalizations and methodological leads, and turning a succession of those leads into patentable or marketable technologies is qualitatively different. If the counterfactual is “without this archive, this commercially valuable development probably would not have happened in this form or at this time,” then asking for a livable share of the resulting value is entirely compatible with having made the research freely available.\n\nI'd therefore restructure the eventual commercial provision around three levels:\n\n**Ordinary / exploratory commercial use:** generous standing permission, attribution, no payment.\n\n**Material SAT-dependent commercial use:** attribution plus a reasonable commercial license whose compensation can take forms such as royalties, a lump sum, equity, research support, or another negotiated arrangement. The exact threshold remains TBD.\n\n**Exceptional or infrastructure-scale use:** the personal compensation obligation remains, but an additional commons/public-benefit component becomes appropriate.             "Yes. That fits the philosophy, but I would make one important wording change: if sending money gives the sender additional legal rights, I would not call it a pure “donation.” It is at least partly consideration for a license. We can call it a **Founding Patron contribution** or **Early Archive Supporter grant**. And unless there is eventually a qualifying nonprofit involved, we should explicitly say it is not represented as tax-deductible.\n\nThe attractive structure is: someone who backs the archive *before anyone knows whether it amounts to anything* gets a materially better deal than somebody who waits until SAT has generated obvious commercial value and then starts mining it.\n\nThat seems fair and gives the archive a way to help you now.\n\nI’d add something like this:\n\n---\n\n### Founding Patron / Early Archive Supporter License\n\nThe archive holder wishes to recognize individuals and organizations that materially support the continued development, preservation, and public availability of the SB2325 archive before its future value is known.\n\nA person or organization making a one-time qualifying support contribution of:\n\n**[FOUNDING PATRON CONTRIBUTION — TBD]**\n\nthrough:\n\n**[CASH APP / OTHER SUPPORT LINK — TBD]**\n\nmay request designation as an **SB2325 Founding Patron**.\n\nUpon acknowledgment of that designation, the Founding Patron receives an additional license to Covered Material first released during:\n\n**[ELIGIBLE FUTURE PERIOD — e.g. lifetime of archive / through a specified date / specified releases — TBD]**\n\nThe intention is that, for the Founding Patron, future Covered Material remains substantially as open to use as the earlier SB2325 archive was intended to be.\n\nSubject to the exclusions below, a Founding Patron may:\n\n- study, copy, preserve, adapt, formalize, test, implement, publish, and build upon Covered Material;\n- use Covered Material in commercial as well as noncommercial activity;\n- retain that permission even if the archive's ordinary commercial terms later become more restrictive;\n- and continue using material received under this grant under the terms applicable when the Founding Patron right attached.\n\nReasonable attribution and provenance remain required.\n\nThe Founding Patron license does **not**:\n\n- transfer ownership of the archive;\n- convey rights in third-party material;\n- convey rights the archive holder does not possess;\n- grant patent rights unless expressly stated;\n- authorize false claims of authorship or origin;\n- authorize use of separately licensed music, artwork, software, or other excluded material contrary to its own license;\n- or imply endorsement by Nathan McKnight / Nathan J. Bellomy.\n\n### Relationship to commercial reciprocity\n\nA Founding Patron is exempt from:\n\n**[WHICH ORDINARY COMMERCIAL THRESHOLD / NEGOTIATION REQUIREMENTS ARE WAIVED — TBD]**\n\nfor Covered Material within the scope of the Founding Patron grant.\n\nHowever:\n\n**[TBD: DOES THE EXCEPTIONAL-SCALE COMMONS-RECIPROCITY CONDITION STILL APPLY?]**\n\nThe archive holder's present preference is that early support should buy genuine long-term freedom rather than merely a discount on later licensing.\n\n### Personal or organizational status\n\nFounding Patron status is granted to:\n\n**[NAMED INDIVIDUAL / NAMED LEGAL ENTITY — TBD RULE]**\n\nand is:\n\n**[NONTRANSFERABLE / TRANSFERABLE WITH BUSINESS SUCCESSOR / OTHER — TBD].**\n\nIt may not be purchased nominally by one party solely to sublicense the entire archive to unrelated third parties unless expressly agreed.\n\n### No retroactive repricing\n\nOnce granted, a Founding Patron license cannot be withdrawn merely because SB2325 or its derivatives later become unexpectedly valuable.\n\nThe whole point of the program is to recognize support provided while that value remained uncertain.\n\n### Support contribution\n\nA Founding Patron contribution supports the archive holder and continued archive work.\n\nIt should not be represented as a charitable or tax-deductible donation unless a qualifying charitable entity is subsequently established and expressly receives it as such.\n\n---\n\nI particularly like the **no retroactive repricing** provision. Imagine somebody gives you $5,000 when SAT is still an enormous weird GitHub archive nobody knows what to do with. Fifteen years later some part turns out to matter enormously. It would be contrary to the whole point to say, “Oops, now your early-patron license costs $20 million.” They took the uncertainty with you.\n\nBut I would **not automatically make it literally MIT-equivalent**. The existing MIT root license is extraordinarily broad: among other things it permits sublicensing and selling copies of the licensed material. fileciteturn268file0L2-L2 A $5,000 supporter shouldn't necessarily gain the ability to package the entire future SB2325 corpus, sell unlimited archive licenses to Microsoft, and become your competing licensor.\n\nWhat I think you actually mean by “like the current archive” is closer to:\n\n> **They personally/organizationally get very broad freedom to use the future work, including commercially, permanently and without later royalties, provided they preserve attribution.**\n\nThat is a very valuable right without allowing them to become a wholesaler of your future licensing rights.\n\nAnd there is an interesting moral symmetry here. The later giant commercial user pays because it **waited for uncertainty to collapse into value**. The early patron gets favorable treatment because it put meaningful resources into keeping the work alive while the value was still unresolved.\n\nSo this becomes almost an **early risk-sharing tier**, not simply a tip jar.\n\nThe big decisions for this section are only four:\n\n1. **How much is “a good chunk of change”?**\n2. **Does it cover all future SB2325 material indefinitely, or a defined period?**\n3. **Does it exempt the patron even from the exceptional-scale commons obligation, or only from your personal commercial-compensation requirement?**\n4. **Can organizations buy it, and if so should their price be different from an individual's?**\n\nI suspect #4 matters a lot. A $2,000 lifetime license for an individual researcher could be generous and sensible; exactly the same $2,000 lifetime license purchased today by Google would be a rather different proposition."

            "Yes. That gives us a much cleaner access structure, and it separates **permission to research/mine SAT** from **permission to commercially exploit something discovered through it**. I would write the relevant portion roughly like this:\n\n---\n\n## Research and Academic Open Access\n\nUse of the SB2325 Theoretical Sandbox for independent research, individual academic work, academic research programmes, teaching, scholarship, criticism, testing, formalization, simulation, and other bona fide academic or research purposes is free and open.\n\nNo fee, subscription, or separate permission is required.\n\nThis remains true regardless of institutional affiliation or funding source, provided the use is genuinely research or academic in character and is not being conducted principally as part of a plan to create, develop, or operate a commercial business based upon the Covered Material or resulting developments.\n\nReasonable attribution and provenance remain expected.\n\nIn plain language:\n\n> **Research it for free. Study it for free. Teach it for free. Build a research programme around it for free. If the intention becomes building a business from it, the commercial terms begin to apply.**\n\n---\n\n## Commercial Research — Early Supporter Open Access Pass\n\nA commercial researcher, company, laboratory, research organization, or other commercial entity may obtain an **Early Supporter Open Access Pass** for a one-time contribution of:\n\n**US $5,000**\n\nThe pass grants broad continuing access to the Covered Material for commercial research and development purposes, subject to reasonable attribution.\n\nA condition of the Early Supporter Pass is that substantive research findings arising from use of the archive be made openly available to the public within a reasonable period, subject to legitimate temporary limitations involving safety, security, privacy, regulatory obligations, or protection of genuinely independent inventions.\n\nThe intent is:\n\n> **Support the archive early, use it broadly, and keep the resulting research conversation open.**\n\nThe $5,000 contribution is consideration for an additional commercial research license and should not be represented as a tax-deductible charitable donation unless separately qualified as such.\n\nThe Early Supporter Pass is:\n\n**[TBD: permanently available, or available only until a specified date/archive milestone.]**\n\n---\n\n## Commercial Archive Mining / Open Research Access\n\nA substantial commercial organization wishing to systematically search, computationally mine, analyze, ingest, or otherwise use SB2325 as a continuing source of research directions, technical structures, methods, formalizations, or potentially exploitable developments may obtain a commercial open-access research license for:\n\n**US $10,000 per annum**\n\nThis permits continuing commercial research access to the Covered Material during the paid period.\n\nReasonable attribution and preservation of provenance remain required.\n\nThe annual license permits commercial **research and mining**. It does not constitute a buyout of all rights relating to commercially significant technologies subsequently derived from the archive.\n\nSo, yes:\n\n> **If Google wants to mine SB2325 as an R&D resource: $10,000/year.**\n\nThat is deliberately modest relative to the scale of such an organization. Its purpose is not to make access economically difficult. It establishes that systematic corporate extraction is a licensed relationship rather than an unreciprocated appropriation of the archive.\n\n---\n\n## Commercialization of Results Is Separate\n\nNeither the $5,000 Early Supporter Pass nor the $10,000 annual Commercial Research Access license automatically settles the treatment of major downstream commercial value.\n\nThey authorize **research access and use of the archive**.\n\nIf that research subsequently produces a product, patent portfolio, platform, process, technology, or other commercial development that becomes materially dependent upon identifiable SB2325 / RMS / SAT / H(s)H contributions and generates substantial private value, the Material SAT-Dependent Commercial Use provisions apply separately.\n\nThus:\n\n> **$10,000/year buys Google permission to mine the field. It does not buy Google the field.**\n\nOrdinary developments of modest commercial significance remain covered by the commercial safe harbor.\n\nSubstantial SAT-dependent commercialization requires a fair separate arrangement providing meaningful economic participation to Nathan McKnight / Nathan J. Bellomy.\n\nExceptional-scale applications additionally trigger the Commons Reciprocity provisions.\n\n---\n\nI think that resolves something that had been muddy in the earlier draft. There are now **three different transactions**, not one sliding commercial-license fee:\n\n**Research access:** essentially free to the research world.\n\n**Systematic commercial research access:** $5,000 once for qualifying early supporters who publish their findings openly, or $10,000/year for ongoing corporate mining.\n\n**Successful commercialization:** only becomes a separate economic issue when something resulting from that research actually crosses our still-to-be-defined significance/dependence threshold.\n\nThat means a pharmaceutical company could pay $10K/year, spend five years searching SAT, find absolutely nothing useful, and owe you nothing further. That's sensible.\n\nIf instead they pay $10K/year, discover an SAT-derived mechanism that becomes the basis of a $4-billion business, the absurd result is *not* “great, we bought Nathan's contribution for ten grand.” The access license got them legitimately through the door; the successful downstream commercial relationship is a different question.\n\nWe now have only a few substantial numerical questions left: **what counts as ordinary commercial safe-harbor value, what triggers Material SAT-Dependent Commercial Use, and what compensation principle applies after that trigger.** The $5K and $10K research-access tiers are now concrete."
